## Saved files and live objects

::: {.computing-flow}
**Disk**: `data/seedlings.csv` + `R/inspect_seedlings.R`

↓ Run the script; read the file

**R memory**: `seedlings` data frame → `diameter` vector

↓ Execute the plotting command

**Output**: a plot; a saved report when explicitly rendered
:::

The same name can refer to very different things: a file, an object or a column.

::: notes
0–3 minutes, including title. Ask which of these survives closing R without
saving a workspace. Files that were saved remain; objects must be recreated.
The default plot is displayed, not automatically saved to disk.
:::

## A project folder and its files

::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
```text
AFEC-R-foundations/
├── AFEC-R-foundations.Rproj
├── data/
│   └── seedlings.csv
├── R/
│   └── inspect_seedlings.R
├── report.qmd
└── report.html
```
:::
::: {.column width="46%"}

| Extension | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `.Rproj` | RStudio Project settings |
| `.csv` | Tabular data as text |
| `.R` | Saved R instructions |
| `.qmd` | Prose and executable code |
| `.html` | A document viewed in a browser |

:::
:::

Files can live in different subfolders within one project.

::: notes
3–6 minutes. Show the extracted folder and reveal extensions in the file manager
if hidden. Folder names are conventions, not special R syntax. Changing a file
extension alone does not convert its contents. Keep data unchanged and save
instructions separately. Quarto uses Markdown for the prose; no syntax lesson.
:::

## Paths need a starting point

**Working directory:** the folder R uses to resolve relative file paths.

| Path | Starting point |
|---|---|
| `data/seedlings.csv` | Current working directory |
| `C:/research/AFEC-R-foundations/data/seedlings.csv` | Drive root (Windows example) |
| `/home/research/AFEC-R-foundations/data/seedlings.csv` | Filesystem root (Linux example) |

```{.r}
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
```

If the whole project moves, which path can stay the same?

::: notes
6–10 minutes. Absolute paths are illustrative, not commands or participant
requirements. macOS absolute paths also start with /. Use / inside quoted R
paths on all classroom systems. In browser RStudio, paths refer to the server's
filesystem; uploading/extracting makes files available there. Relative paths
remain valid when the whole folder moves and R starts at the new project root.
The file.exists result is FALSE if the starting point or file name is wrong.
:::

## RStudio: instructions, execution and results

| Source editor | Environment |
|---|---|
| Edit and save `R/inspect_seedlings.R` | Inspect objects created in this R session |
| **Console** | **Files / Plots** |
| Execute commands; read output and errors | Browse saved files / view plots |

R runs code in the Console when you send it from Source with **Run**.

The Files pane can browse a folder without changing R's working directory.

::: notes
10–14 minutes. The table is a schematic of the common pane layout, not a
screenshot; actual layouts differ. Point to these panes in the live IDE.
Brief checks in the Console are useful. Save the analysis instructions in a
script so their order can be inspected and rerun. Console history can persist,
but it is not a substitute for an intentional analysis script.
:::

## Opening a Project establishes context

Open `AFEC-R-foundations.Rproj`, then open `R/inspect_seedlings.R`.

```{.r}
getwd()
file.exists("data/seedlings.csv")
```

- Opening the Project sets the initial working directory to its folder.
- The relative path then works even though the script is inside `R/`.
- Reopen the Project and check `getwd()` if a file cannot be found.

A Project organizes the work; the script recreates its objects.

::: notes
14–19 minutes. Demonstrate on the prepared Project, not in the parent repository.
Confirm Project name and actual getwd output. No setwd or machine-specific
paths in the script. The working directory can later be changed explicitly;
a Project is not a permanent lock on it. Merely opening a script does not change
it. Do not teach Project creation menus: provide the functioning Project.
Source: https://docs.posit.co/ide/user/ide/guide/code/projects.html
:::

## Saving code and running code

```{.r}
diameter <- c(2.1, 3.4, 4.7)
diameter
```

| Action | What changes? |
|---|---|
| Save the script | Instructions on disk |
| Run the assignment | An object named `diameter` in memory |
| Run `diameter` | Its values appear in the Console |

After a fresh R session, saved instructions must run again to recreate objects.

::: notes
19–22 minutes. Predict which pane changes after Save vs Run; show the difference.
Do not repeat the Harry/Potter arithmetic drills. If time permits restart R and
rerun the two lines; otherwise describe this and do one restart in the practical.
The supplied Project disables workspace restore/save. A Project alone does not
save data objects or guarantee reproducibility. Saving a script also does not
save its most recent printed results.
:::

## Reading a CSV creates an object

```{.r}
seedlings <- read.csv("data/seedlings.csv")
```

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"data/seedlings.csv"` | A path to a saved input file |
| `read.csv(...)` | Read the file and return a data frame |
| `seedlings <-` | Assign that result to an object named `seedlings` |

R uses the in-memory object for subsequent inspection and plotting.
Editing that object does not automatically rewrite the CSV.

::: notes
22–25 minutes. Distinguish the quotes from the unquoted object name and case.
Explain right side evaluated before assignment. Reading again refreshes the
object from disk; running a later plotting line does not automatically reread a
changed CSV. CSV is one supported format, not the only format R can read.
Source: R read.table/read.csv documentation.
:::

## Data type and data structure

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
### Type of values

- **Numeric:** `2.1`, `3.4` mm.
- **Character:** `"Species_A"`.
- **Logical:** `TRUE`, `FALSE`.

`NA` marks a missing value in a column.
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
### Organization of values

- **Vector:** a sequence of values.
- **Data frame:** a table of columns.

The columns here are vectors of equal length. Each column has its own type.
:::
:::

A numeric column and a data frame describe different aspects of the data.

::: notes
25–29 minutes. Restrict vector here to ordinary atomic vectors, each with one
underlying type. A general list can mix object types; a data frame is a list of
columns with equal row counts. This one sentence is enough; no list exercise.
In R numeric usually means double here. If asked, 30 is numeric/double whereas
30L is integer; storage type does not determine a variable's scientific role.
NA is an indicator, not a separate ordinary measurement type.
:::

## Observations, columns and their types

```{r preview}
head(seedlings, 3)
```

One row follows **one tagged seedling** over one observation interval.
Columns describe its ID, species, initial stem diameter and later survival.

```{r structure}
str(seedlings)
```

::: notes
29–33 minutes. The data are fictional, not a subset of Day 1–3's model data.
Species_A/Species_B are fictional labels. Read 8 observations, 4 variables, chr,
num and logi aloud. Several rows can have the same species. These are seedling
stem diameters in mm, not adult DBH. The preview deliberately requests 3 rows;
head(seedlings) without that argument shows six by default.
:::

## A column is a vector

```{r column}
diameter <- seedlings$diameter_mm
class(seedlings)
class(diameter)
length(diameter)
```

`seedlings$diameter_mm` selects a **column**, with one entry per seedling.

```{r mixed-vector}
class(c(2.1, "unmeasured"))
```

Mixing a number and text in this vector makes both entries character values.

::: notes
33–37 minutes. class identifies an object's class, not a complete specification
of its internal storage; no typeof detour. Show that "unmeasured" in an otherwise
numeric CSV column may change its imported class too. Keep numeric measurement
and missingness separate. This is one demonstration of coercion, not a type
conversion tutorial. The assignment copies values semantically; it creates no
live link that writes back to the data frame or input file.
:::

## Missing is different from zero or death

```{r missing}
is.na(diameter)
seedlings$survived
```

- Missing diameter: no recorded measurement, not a diameter of zero.
- `survived = FALSE`: observed dead at the later census.
- `survived = NA`: survival status was not recorded.

`is.na()` identifies missing entries; it returns a logical vector.

::: notes
37–41 minutes. Missing diameter is record 4; missing survival is record 5.
The input token NA becomes a missing marker with this import function. The text
"NA" in an R character vector is distinct from R's missing marker. Do not
substitute 0 or FALSE for unknown values or introduce imputation here.
Source: https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/NA.html
:::

## Inspection before interpretation

| Command | What to inspect |
|---|---|
| `class(seedlings)` | The class of the whole object |
| `str(seedlings)` | Structure, column classes/types and example entries |
| `head(seedlings)` | First six records by default |
| `dim(seedlings)` | Rows, then columns |

Which command would reveal a diameter column imported as text?

A preview of six rows does not remove the remaining rows from the object.

::: notes
41–45 minutes. str reveals the column type; class of the whole table alone does
not. A numeric-looking printed value is not enough evidence. Ask for a reason,
not recall of syntax. Scientific interpretation also needs the data dictionary
and units. Do not reteach names, levels, summary and tail as a second catalogue.
:::

## Guided practical: files, objects and a plot

Open `exercise.html` and the prepared script `R/inspect_seedlings.R`.

1. Locate the Project, data file and script; verify the working directory.
2. Run the import and inspect the table and a column.
3. Interpret missing observations; run the supplied histogram.

Explain where the input lives, what R holds in memory, and what each row means.

All code is supplied. The rendered handout provides the same outputs if R is unavailable.

::: notes
45–58 minutes: allow 3 location, 4 import/inspection, 3 columns/NA and 3 plot.
Reserve 58–60 for the recap/questions. Students work in pairs if needed; no new
code required. If a setup problem lasts two minutes, switch to supplied outputs
and return to the folder diagram. The histogram uses seven measured diameters.
:::

## Optional: a Quarto document {visibility="uncounted"}

`report.qmd`: Markdown prose + R code → **Render** → `report.html`

- The QMD records how to generate the report.
- The HTML displays its text, code and plot in a browser.
- The prepared report reads its own CSV; Console objects are unnecessary.

Use the prepared HTML if Quarto is unavailable. No installation is needed today.

::: notes
Only if the practical finishes early: replace up to two minutes of spare
practical/demo time. Never extend the hour. The report QMD is at the participant
Project root, so its default document-directory execution finds data/. This is
different from running an R/ script interactively with the project-root working
directory. No execution-directory settings or Markdown syntax lesson for students.
Source: https://quarto.org/docs/projects/code-execution.html
:::

## Recreating the analysis

Keep the input CSV, saved script and data dictionary in the Project folder.

A fresh session can recreate the objects by running the script from the top.

For research handoff, also record the software environment and preserve backups.
A Project supplies context; it does not do those jobs automatically.

::: notes
58–60 minutes, including questions. Ask a participant to trace CSV -> data frame
-> diameter vector -> plot using actual filenames and objects. Do not add another
exercise. No statistical inference or model explanation in this session.
:::
